query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The application of cold roll bonding to W-Cu composites can improve their mechanical properties and thermal transport by reducing defects and enhancing the distribution of W reinforcements in the Cu matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: W-Cu composite with defects and imperfect W distribution
generation.structural_mediator: W reinforcement distribution and density of dislocations
generation.mechanism: Dislocation generation and interaction, Orowan strengthening, and whisker alignment
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate strength) and thermal transport
generation.boundary: Limited by the processing temperature and rolling reductions
generation.uncertainty: The exact effect of cold roll bonding on W-Cu composites is uncertain and requires experimental verification

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment with varying rolling reductions and temperature conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the application of cold roll bonding does not result in improved mechanical properties and thermal transport, the hypothesis is falsified.

The most important advantage is that the non-wetting metals and reinforcements can be combined in this process. Thus, a wide diversity of materials can be used. Additionally, this method provides better control of preform and melt temperature compared to pressureless infiltration methods. Furthermore, selective solidification can be obtained in this process. In contrast to die pressure infiltration casting, it does not need pressure die. Better distribution of reinforcements in metal matrix and more controlled reactions can be achieved through this method [,].
It is widely acknowledged that ceramic-metal composites present superior mechanical properties, and tribological performance than unreinforced composites [,,]. Among many hard reinforcements, SiC with high wear resistance and thermal stability are well suited in metal matrix composites []. Thus, the addition of SiC to metal-based composite can enable MMCs to be used in applications involving chemically aggressive media, tribological stresses, and high temperatures [,]. ## Characterization of composites’ microstructures
Fig. 2(a–c) show the images taken from whiskers, raw Al sheet, and Cu billet, respectively. As illustrated in Fig. 2d, the microstructure of Cu–SiC shows the distribution of SiC whiskers in the copper matrix. However, the whiskers were locally agglomerated across the matrix. This agglomeration is a typical feature of ceramic-metal composites produced by infiltration methods. Owing to reducing the interfacial energy, the whiskers agglomeration occurs []. It is also believed that poor wettability of whiskers is responsible for agglomeration. However, Cook and Werner [] found out that pressure infiltration can overcome the poor wettability between ceramics and metals. ## Investigation of grain structure
The EBSD images of the Al layer and Cu–SiC layer before and after rolling is shown in Fig. 4(a–h). The grain size of layers after the rolling process experienced two major changes. The average grain size of Al and Cu–SiC layers decreases. Also, the grains became elongated toward the rolling direction. These elongation values are much higher than those reported by Qiu et al. [] who produced SiC/Al–Cu composite by semisolid stirring with ball milling technology. The increase in strength values and decrease in elongation values have been reported in the literature []. They are related to the increased density of dislocations during the rolling process. Then, dislocation movement is limited due to the dislocation's interaction. The dislocation movement is further limited by SiC whiskers. Therefore, in ceramic-metal composites higher strengths and lower ductility exist compared to metal-metal composites or metal sheets. In ceramic-metal composites, the increase in dislocations is often caused by elastic modulus mismatch, thermal expansion mismatch, and Orowan strengthening [, , ]. These are also affected by the content, shape, and distribution of ceramic reinforcement and the quality of interfaces between ceramic and metal.
